title: Quantifiers: Much, Many, Few, Little and Plenty
summary: Choose quantifiers for countable and uncountable nouns, use much or a lot naturally in different kinds of sentences, and distinguish an insufficient amount (few/little) from a small but useful amount (a few/a little). Use plenty of for more than enough and keep only with the positive small-quantity forms.
learningObjectives: Use much and little with uncountable nouns and many and few with plural countable nouns.
Choose much in negatives and questions and prefer a lot of or lots of in ordinary positive statements when appropriate.
Explain the difference in meaning between few/a few and little/a little using context.
Use plenty of, plenty to, only a few and only a little appropriately to describe quantity and adequacy.

explanation.heading: Countability determines the quantifier
explanation.body: Use much and (a) little with uncountable nouns such as equipment, patience and information. Use many and (a) few with plural countable nouns such as requests, colleagues and tickets. A lot of, lots of and plenty of can go before either kind of noun. Do not attach many to an uncountable noun or much to a plural countable noun when describing quantity.
explanation.example: There is little room in the storage cupboard, but there are many boxes to put away.

explanation.heading: Much in questions and negatives; a lot in statements
explanation.body: Much is very common in questions and negative sentences: Did it require much effort? and It did not require much effort. Ordinary affirmative sentences often prefer a lot of rather than much by itself: The repair required a lot of effort. Affirmative too much, so much and as much remain natural. Many is possible in affirmative, interrogative and negative statements. For frequent time expressions, many years or many weeks is especially natural.
explanation.example: We have not received much feedback, although we have collected a lot of survey responses.

explanation.heading: Plenty means more than enough
explanation.body: Plenty of is stronger than merely some or a lot of: it says the quantity is sufficient, usually with extra to spare. It works with both plural countable and uncountable nouns: plenty of chairs and plenty of time. When the meaning is an available activity or opportunity rather than a noun quantity, use plenty to + verb: plenty to explore, plenty to discuss. Plenty of is not necessarily an exact measurement.
explanation.example: We have plenty of volunteers, so every visitor can be shown around.

explanation.heading: Few and little emphasise a shortage
explanation.body: Few with plural nouns and little with uncountable nouns usually suggest less than the speaker considers desirable. Few applicants responded suggests a disappointing number; little progress suggests a disappointing amount. Very few and very little strengthen this negative interpretation. The surrounding situation can change the evaluation, but without an article the quantity is usually presented as limited.
explanation.example: The organisers had little information about the delay, so they could not update the guests.

explanation.heading: A few and a little emphasise some available quantity
explanation.body: A few refers to a small number and a little to a small amount; both often suggest that something exists and may be enough for a purpose. Compare few minutes (hardly any) with a few minutes (some time). The article a changes the message even though the quantity may be small. Say only a few or only a little, not only few or only little, when the meaning is a small specified quantity.
explanation.example: We still have a few minutes before the talk begins, so there is time for one question.

left.label: Uncountable: much/little
left.example: We have little evidence for that claim.
left.note: Evidence is uncountable; little points to an insufficient amount.

right.label: Plural countable: many/few
right.example: We have few photographs of the event.
right.note: Photographs are countable; few suggests an insufficient number.

left.label: Little: less than desired
left.example: There is little daylight left, so we must stop work.
left.note: Little highlights a shortage and suggests the work cannot continue.

right.label: A little: some remains
right.example: There is a little daylight left, so we can finish this task.
right.note: A little highlights some available time, even though the amount is small.

comparisons.title: Much versus a lot of in everyday statements

left.label: Question with much
left.example: Did the training require much preparation?
left.note: Much is natural in a question about uncountable preparation.

right.label: Affirmative with a lot of
right.example: The training required a lot of preparation.
right.note: A lot of is idiomatic in an ordinary affirmative sentence.

examples.sentence: How much luggage can you take on this flight?
examples.note: Luggage is uncountable; much asks about its amount.

examples.sentence: The editor made many suggestions before approving the article.
examples.note: Suggestions is plural countable, so many fits.

examples.sentence: There is plenty of space for the new equipment.
examples.note: Plenty of implies that the space is more than sufficient.

examples.sentence: I know few people in this neighbourhood, which makes settling in difficult.
examples.note: Few presents the small number of acquaintances as a disadvantage.

examples.sentence: We have a little paint left, enough to cover the final shelf.
examples.note: A little signals a useful amount of an uncountable substance.

examples.sentence: Only a few passengers had boarded when the announcement was made.
examples.note: Only a few describes a small number and keeps the article a.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The team has many equipment to move.
commonMistakes.correct: The team has a lot of equipment to move.
commonMistakes.why: Equipment is uncountable; use a lot of, not many.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We have much free time this afternoon.
commonMistakes.correct: We have a lot of free time this afternoon.
commonMistakes.why: In an ordinary affirmative statement, a lot of is more natural than bare much.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have few minutes, so I can answer one short question.
commonMistakes.correct: I have a few minutes, so I can answer one short question.
commonMistakes.why: A few highlights some available minutes; few by itself usually stresses an inadequate number.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Only little water remains in the bottle.
commonMistakes.correct: Only a little water remains in the bottle.
commonMistakes.why: Use only a little to describe a small remaining amount of an uncountable noun.

studyTips: Classify nouns as plural countable or uncountable before choosing much/many or little/few.
Create paired situations where a small amount is disappointing versus useful; practise few/a few and little/a little aloud.
Change three neutral quantity questions into natural affirmative statements, using much in questions and a lot of in statements; add plenty of only when the amount is more than enough.

exercises.prompt: The new system stores ___ information about each order, so we need extra storage space.
exercises.feedback: Information is uncountable and the sentence is affirmative, so a lot of is natural.

exercises.prompt: We cannot print the report because there is ___ paper left in the office.
exercises.feedback: Paper here is uncountable, and little emphasises an insufficient supply.

exercises.prompt: The waiting room has forty seats but only six visitors. There are ___ seats available.
exercises.feedback: Plenty of indicates more seats than are needed and works with the plural noun seats.

exercises.prompt: We can still discuss one more issue before lunch because we have ___.
exercises.feedback: Time is uncountable; a little time shows that some time remains and is usable.

exercises.prompt: The archivist found ___ photographs of the building, so reconstructing its history was difficult. (one word meaning not many)
exercises.feedback: Few with plural photographs stresses a shortage of useful pictures.

exercises.prompt: Could you lend me ___ coins for the parking meter? Three would be enough. (two words meaning a small number)
exercises.feedback: A few describes some countable coins, enough for the stated purpose.

exercises.prompt: We have ___ chairs for every guest, with several left over. (two-word expression meaning more than enough)
exercises.feedback: Plenty of before a plural noun says that the number of chairs exceeds what is required.

exercises.prompt: There is ___ sugar in this sauce, so it does not taste sweet. (one word meaning not much)
exercises.feedback: Little modifies uncountable sugar and points to a low quantity.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: How many advice did the mentor give you?
acceptedAnswers: How much advice did the mentor give you?
exercises.feedback: Advice is uncountable, so ask how much advice, not how many advice.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We spent many money on the conference last week.
acceptedAnswers: We spent a lot of money on the conference last week.
exercises.feedback: Money is uncountable, so many money is incorrect. A lot of money is natural in an affirmative sentence.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We only need few minutes to check the figures.
acceptedAnswers: We only need a few minutes to check the figures.
exercises.feedback: Use only a few with a small number of countable minutes.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: There are very little buses after midnight.
acceptedAnswers: There are very few buses after midnight.
exercises.feedback: Buses is plural and countable; very few, not very little, describes their low number.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one sentence from these facts: the team / have / many requests / this morning. Use the present simple and begin with “The team”.
acceptedAnswers: The team has many requests this morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Many works with the plural countable noun requests.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a yes/no question starting with “Did” from these facts: the repair / require / much work.
acceptedAnswers: Did the repair require much work?
speakingExercises.feedback: Much is natural in a question about the uncountable noun work.

speakingExercises.prompt: Rephrase this sentence using “a lot of” without changing its meaning: “The festival attracted many visitors.” Begin with “The festival”.
acceptedAnswers: The festival attracted a lot of visitors.
speakingExercises.feedback: A lot of can quantify the plural noun visitors in an affirmative sentence.

speakingExercises.prompt: The cupboard is almost empty and the cooking cannot begin. Say one sentence using exactly: “There is” / “little flour” / “left”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Little with uncountable flour communicates an inadequate amount.

speakingExercises.prompt: You can make one final call before leaving. Say one sentence beginning “I have”, using “a little time” and ending “before I leave”.
acceptedAnswers: I have a little time before I leave.
speakingExercises.feedback: A little time emphasises a small but usable amount of time.

speakingExercises.prompt: There are more pens than participants. Say one sentence using “We have”, “plenty of pens” and “for everyone”.
acceptedAnswers: We have plenty of pens for everyone.
speakingExercises.feedback: Plenty of says that the supply is more than enough.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences, in this order. Facts: we / have / few volunteers; we / need / more help. Use the present simple and a full form of the second sentence.
acceptedAnswers: We have few volunteers. We need more help.
speakingExercises.feedback: Few volunteers describes a shortage; the second sentence states its consequence.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the quantity expression and say the full corrected sentence, changing nothing else: “Only few tickets remain for the morning session.”
acceptedAnswers: Only a few tickets remain for the morning session.
speakingExercises.feedback: After only, a few expresses the small remaining number of tickets.

listeningExercises.audioText: The organisers had very few helpers, so everyone had to manage two different tasks.
listeningExercises.prompt: What problem did the organisers face?
choices: They had more helpers than they needed.
They had too few people to share the work easily.
They had no tasks to assign.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very few helpers indicates a shortage, explaining why each person handled multiple tasks.

listeningExercises.audioText: We only have a little time before the next lecture, but we can still get a quick coffee.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker mean about the time available?
choices: There is some time for a brief activity.
There is no time for anything.
There is enough time for a long lunch.
listeningExercises.feedback: A little time and the planned quick coffee imply a small but usable amount.

listeningExercises.audioText: There is very little sunlight in this courtyard during winter afternoons.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression immediately before “sunlight”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very little describes an extremely small amount of uncountable sunlight.

listeningExercises.audioText: The tour starts in an hour, and we have plenty of time to visit the exhibition first.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why is the exhibition visit possible?
choices: The speaker has cancelled the tour.
There is more than enough time before the tour.
listeningExercises.feedback: Plenty of time means sufficient time with extra to spare.

listeningExercises.audioText: Did the new equipment need much maintenance? No, hardly any, according to the engineer.
listeningExercises.prompt: How often or extensively does the equipment need attention?
choices: It needs more maintenance than expected.
listeningExercises.feedback: Hardly any maintenance means almost none, matching the negative reply.

listeningExercises.audioText: The committee received many suggestions, but only a few were practical enough to adopt.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the committee say about the suggestions?
choices: Many arrived, but only a small number were usable.
listeningExercises.feedback: Many contrasts a large number received with a few practical options.

listeningExercises.audioText: I need a few extra minutes to complete the application carefully.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantifier immediately before “extra minutes”.
listeningExercises.feedback: A few quantifies a small number of additional minutes.

listeningExercises.audioText: There are plenty of rooms for everyone attending the overnight workshop.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression immediately before “rooms”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Plenty of means there are more than enough rooms.
